title: Google tech writing: error messages, set the tone
rule: Say how to get it right, not what the user did wrong; no blame; no humour; apologise sparingly, and no 'please'.
example: Not: 'You didn't enter a name.' / 'We're sorry, a server error occurred and we're temporarily unable to load your spreadsheet.' Yes: 'Enter a name.' / 'Google Docs is temporarily unable to open your spreadsheet.' + a workaround
llm_tell: Reflexive 'Sorry'/'Oops'/'We couldn't...' openers and jokes in errors are the default model register.

title: Intuit content design: errors
rule: Plain language at about 5th-8th grade level; skip error codes (log them); be specific, give timing if known; limit 'try again' to cases with no more specific action; match tone to severity (casual only for minor); handle 'error, oops, wrong, invalid, fail' with care. 'We' is fine when it is our fault and relevant.
example: Do: 'Try reducing this file to 30 MB or less.' Don't: 'Your file's too big.' Fault-ours: 'We need to fix some things on our end. Sign out and try again later.'
llm_tell: Same 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' for every failure is the model default; Intuit asks for the specific action.

title: Atlassian: error messages
rule: Error only after an action (warning for a condition that may cause trouble). Explain what happened, consequence, next step, in 1-2 sentences. Title 3-4 words, doesn't tell what to do; body doesn't repeat title. Don't invent a cause: if unknown say something went wrong and offer a next step. Avoid 'sorry' (makes error seem severe) and 'please' (makes a required step sound optional). CTA is an imperative verb, not 'OK'; offer a dismiss.
example: Page's examples are images; the fetch tool's table was its own illustration, not quoted. Unknown cause: 'Something went wrong. Try again, or contact support if it keeps happening.' (illustration)
llm_tell: Invented plausible causes ('due to a network timeout') are a model habit; the rule forbids guessing.

title: Atlassian vs Google/Intuit on 'we'/'you'
rule: DISAGREEMENT: Atlassian page text (full read) says address the reader as 'you' not 'we' because 'we' can make people feel responsible; a search snippet of the same site paraphrased it the opposite way, so treat the pronoun rule as unresolved. Intuit allows 'we' when it is our fault. Google says avoid blaming 'you'. Apology: Atlassian/Google/Salesforce say rare; Microsoft (snippet) allows 'sorry' for burdensome tasks or serious consequences.
llm_tell: Pick one house rule per product; a model drifts between 'we', 'you' and 'sorry' across screens.

title: Shopify Polaris: empty state
rule: Empty-state title is action-oriented; subtitle is conversational and explains what the title or item is; only one primary CTA. Button labels lead with a strong verb, verb+noun, except Save/Close/Cancel/OK.
example: Good: 'Create order', 'Buy shipping label'. Poor: 'New order', 'Buy'.

title: Atlassian: empty state
rule: Short informative title, 1-2 sentence body saying why it is empty and where to go next; CTA is a specific imperative verb of one or two words, not 'OK'. Empty states can celebrate completion.
llm_tell: Exclamatory celebration copy ('All caught up!') on every empty list is the generic version.

title: NN/g: Designing Empty States in Complex Applications
rule: Three jobs: state what the system is doing (no entries vs loading), teach what belongs here and how it gets filled, give a direct path (button, learn-more) to the key task. A message that says what to do without how or where fails. Never show 'No records' while content is still loading.
example: Good: 'There are no records to display for the selected date range.' / 'Star your favorites to list them here.' Bad: 'No Records; Send a request to view details in the workspace.'

title: NN/g: Mobile tutorials
rule: Tutorials for simple apps do not help: 70 users, 4 iOS apps; success 91% (read) vs 94% (skipped), not significant; perceived ease 4.92 vs 5.49 of 7 (p=0.047), tutorial readers found it harder. Spend effort on the interface; use contextual help over manual-style tutorials. Four apps, iOS only.
llm_tell: Model-written onboarding is welcome carousels and feature tours; this is evidence against shipping them.

title: NN/g: Onboarding, skip it when possible
rule: Instructions that must be digested before use cost attention and reduce usability; avoid where possible.

title: Apple HIG: Accessing private data
rule: Apple page itself did not load (HTTP 500; JSON endpoint 404), so this is a search summary. Purpose string: one brief complete sentence, sentence case, active voice, ending in a period, specific about how the app uses the data. App Review rejects vague strings (summary quotes 'App needs microphone access').
example: Summary of Apple's own example: the app records during the night to detect snoring sounds.
llm_tell: Generic 'We need access to your camera to enhance your experience' is the model default and the rejected shape.

title: Alexa: five benchmarks for dialog
rule: Plain words not ten-dollar words; one-breath test (read aloud, if you must pause, cut); vary frequent prompts (write 2-5 variants of the 3-5 prompts users hear every session); contractions and informal phrasing; SSML breaks for pacing.
example: Bad: 'The transaction attempt was not successful.' Good: 'Hmm. Something went wrong with your payment.' Bad: 'I'd like to be able to help you' Good: 'I can help.' Bad: 'Do you want to continue?' Good: 'Ready?'
llm_tell: Uniform full-sentence formality and one fixed greeting per launch.

title: Alexa Voice Design Guide: what Alexa says
rule: Keep responses short since long ones are hard to follow and remember; don't read menus of options, explain what is possible and steer toward useful input.
